Ordinary lifecycle close or eligible terminal reset does not silently release another controller's locks; matching RESUME or permanent release retires them. pausable=false ignores PAUSE/RESUME and creates no effective lock. Pause is not itself activation, cancellation or PULL demand.

Default PAUSE prohibits new fn invocations, including first activation, across source and computed nodes. It does not cancel or hold lawful output of work already started, including registered host callbacks. resumeAll permits fn/input processing but holds eligible output publication in node-local FIFO; terminal/TEARDOWN bypass and terminal discards held publication. Resume does not rerun already-processed hooks/fn for output entries. Finish a started array, apply queued controls at the proper boundary and recheck before the next entry. New output cannot overtake accepted backlog. pausable=false ignores pause controls. No external async cancellation or latest-task-wins strategy is implied. Quiet PULL publication additionally obeys R-pull: RESUME without pending demand does not by itself flush that holder.

Pause behavior depends on invocation versus publication, not sync/async pool labels, dependency count or callback origin. Default PAUSE gates new calls and permits earlier lawful results; resumeAll holds eligible publication. Already registered external work may continue until its owner cancels it. A raw deferred-result author must eventually send DATA,RESOLVED or terminal according to its own protocol responsibility; the substrate does not infer completion from return, a pool label or a generic async-task flag.

Configured bounded replay retains published DATA occurrences in logical oldest-to-newest order, including equal values. Ordinary new subscribers receive that history in their START snapshot before live output, irrespective of whether a PULL request exists elsewhere. Quiet PULL holders suppress subscription replay as well as cache push. Pending publication is not committed replay. Snapshot capacity and retained sequence must both be represented for supported restore; current cache or last wave alone cannot reconstruct history.

Restore validates and installs a checkpoint's represented logical graph state at a safe graph boundary before exposing callbacks or resource reconstruction. It is not fresh activation, a hidden recomputation, or live DATA replay. Preserve represented caches/absence/freshness/terminal, private state and policy, first-call history, received-input evidence, replay, versions and logical graph namespace/observation continuity. Rebuild physical identity, dispatcher bindings, subscriptions, native signals and resources through trusted factories/recipes. New native identity alone does not advance revisions or invalidate logical receipts. Missing/local-only factories and known unsupported pending/closing/executing state reject recoverable capture/restore honestly. Storage loading/decoding stays outside the synchronous core. Ordinary post-restore changes use normal input/output boundaries.

Checkpoint includes the live declared topology/factory configuration and the canonical logical facts for each supported category exactly once. Save retained tagged value/absence, freshness, terminal, private data/policy, first-call and input receipts, selected replay/configuration and revision evidence; derive public status and redundant indexes. Collection-owned backend contributors remain authoritative over derived helper caches. Supported pending-buffer recovery must save remaining logical work, order and continuation meaning, not callback closures or native handles. Unsupported work rejects capture; snapshot need not wait, activate nodes or silently drop work. Preserve logical allocation watermarks, retired names and observation sequence when continuing the same graph namespace; rebuild physical maps and observers.

Rewire is intra-graph and surgical: retained connections preserve identity, received/pending records and leases across reorder; removal retires identity and its dirty contribution; re-add creates a fresh connection. Preserve surviving output, pause locks and first-call history. Pair each changed dependency shape with its explicit fn; fn replacement cancels its old unstarted reattach registration but does not force an extra call. Preflight rejection leaves the installed binding unchanged. After installation, outward acquisition failure marks that attempt abandoned: block new calls, retain acquired release responsibility and earlier lawful work until actual close. No automatic rollback/retry is promised. Mid-fn/self changes use the deferred seam; observer-origin changes queue at R-observer-boundary. Reject self/cyclic/cross-graph wiring and invalid terminal acquisition under the ordinary admission policy.

Reject an actual synchronous reentry into a still-running same-node fn; restore its execution scope on every unwind. Observer-origin output/control/subscription requests instead queue at the completed-wave boundary and are not misclassified as fn reentry. No default cap, implicit yield, dropped request, equality suppression or synthetic protocol ERROR terminates an unbounded sequence of individually completed feedback waves; the composition owns termination. Public batch or subscription acquisition from a raw/sugar/operator fn body is rejected before starting its body/acquisition; declared internal wiring/queued rewire retain their designated seams. Public batch from graph observer, initialization or lifecycle callbacks also rejects before its body executes. Ordinary host batch and explicit host nested-body sharing remain permitted; callback reporting failure after commit does not roll that committed data or otherwise valid tasks back.

An unmatched upstream DIRTY,TEARDOWN,RESUME or PULL drops at a depless terminus. INVALIDATE reaching a depless source acts through normal accepted invalidation/downstream publication; intermediates forward rather than self-invalidate. Matching lock/holder actions use R-up-routing before terminus drop. A matching active PULL holder is invoked when serviceable even if inputs did not change; an inactive holder does not activate or bank demand.

A valid ctx may request self-rewire/upNext for its existing lifecycle. Requests apply as fresh boundary work after the originating fn/wave, subject to batch fate, pause and target/lifetime validity. Same-life rerun does not cancel them; actual close cancels old unexecuted work. Rewire accepted before terminal may apply if ready before automatic retirement, with output still sealed; retirement does not wait indefinitely for blocked work. Resource cleanup must not depend solely on a queued rewire. Public fn replacement has no extra reattach parameter; new fn owns future registrations.

A ctx boundary task caused by an open batch waits for its committed boundary; rollback discards that batch-owned unexecuted task. A still-paused task waits for its applicable final lock release while its life remains valid. Observer-origin requests are separately ordered requests, not automatically owned by the enclosing batch rollback. Already accepted old publication also stays outside ambient batch accumulation. Terminal-ready tasks may finish under R-terminal; actual close cancels the remainder. No raw fn, topology application or acquisition may bypass the designated boundary by directly draining a nested queue.

RESOLVED is a no-DATA-occurrence settlement of an actual announced notification, not value equality and not an obligation to emit after every event. Substrate never substitutes equal DATA with RESOLVED. A serviceable synchronous no-output invocation may be balanced automatically only when its still-open notification is not already covered by accepted output or an immediate terminal postlude. Raw deferred-result authors explicitly own eventual DATA/RESOLVED; no async-task registration is required or inferred from silence. Without an announcement, a no-output path stays silent. Authored DATA and RESOLVED cannot coexist in one output array. Stateful buffers/inners/timers are not by themselves outstanding result debts.

For input pending under default PAUSE, INVALIDATE supersedes that dependency's earlier unconsumed paused DATA and retains the necessary invalidation marker. It does not erase surviving other-dependency input or later DATA, and does not by itself create a fn invocation. This rule does not erase DATA already exposed in an invocation or ordinary nonpaused same-array DATA projections. resumeAll output invalidation uses the acceptance/publication split, not this input supersession policy. Default fn pause does not delay effective local invalidation or its normal downstream publication; only the designated publication-hold mode can defer that publication.

DATA,RESOLVED,effective or ineffective INVALIDATE and dependency terminal each release that connection's outstanding dirty membership at most once. Repeated notification prefixes do not create extra memberships. If terminal is absorbed/delegated and output stays open, remaining eligible input may invoke fn; otherwise balance only an actual still-open output notification under R-resolved-undirty. Never invent a result solely to make a pending count zero, await a blocked call before automatic terminal, or leave a dirty contribution stranded because the dependency ended without DATA.

A PULL holder is quiet outside service: subscription is START-only and incoming changes do not announce downstream DIRTY solely for retained state. A matching PULL at an inactive holder drops without activation or banking. At an active blocked holder retain only the latest unserved demand/params; actual close discards it. First publish eligible older accepted backlog, then recheck current gates/latest demand and consume it only at actual invocation service with ctx.pull installed. Invoke once even without changed dependencies; emit or stay silent according to the helper. Re-quiet after service. RESUME alone creates no demand. Output is ordinary DATA/RESOLVED/terminal, with no protocol ACK, cause tag, cross-request idempotency key or guaranteed DATA response. Releasing a pause lock with no pending PULL does not unconditionally flush a quiet holder's backlog. Demand-gated backlog draining preserves the latest demand until actual holder service.

Upstream control/demand uses declared stable connections. Directed ctx routing resolves the invocation's dependency position to its captured connection; node-origin routing resolves current declared topology. Reorder preserves targets; removal/re-add never retargets old work. Immediate explicit targeting of an invalid connection rejects; valid queued work whose target later becomes invalid drops. Broadcast freezes its candidate connection list and validates each before delivery: skip removed targets, stop when origin authority ends, exclude later-added connections and do not roll back delivered effects. A new explicit node broadcast uses current topology. PULL consumes at the matching holder; RESUME releases a matching lock else forwards; PAUSE acquires at its explicit target. Subsequent hops use their own declared routing.

Within one routed control/demand wave, duplicate arrivals at the same matching PULL holder invoke service at most once. This route-local suppression does not deduplicate separate requests with unchanged data or equal params. Controls preserve ordered request application and declared routing; no global request-history or public correlation field is introduced.

Synthesized balancing RESOLVED follows normal output acceptance, batch and publication-pause boundaries. It carries its originating life and expected still-open notification internally; immediately before any DIRTY prepass/public cache/version/callback effect, discard the entire obsolete compensation if that target no longer applies. A discarded compensation creates no new notification, revision or recursive compensation. Once a valid array starts publication, complete its valid fanout. This target check does not suppress explicit user-authored late DATA/RESOLVED by task identity.

A surviving invocation keeps its input/connection view across later rewire for both sync and async use. Its ctx.down remains node output subject to current lifetime/output authority, not a stale task-result filter. Its directed/broadcast upstream actions preserve captured first-hop connection identity under R-up-routing and never acquire authority over replacement edges. Actual old-life closure revokes that ctx regardless of whether the node object or declared topology survives.

Rewire requested while that node has uncommitted batch output waits until the outer batch outcome. Commit publishes/accepts the old-shape accumulated wave under its existing topology/fn before the queued mutation; rollback discards batch-owned mutations. Observer-origin requests retain their independent ordered fate. No old-shape pending DATA is reinterpreted as input for a replacement dependency shape, and old accepted resumeAll backlog is not enlisted into the new batch.

One callback object identifies one live stream registration; repeated subscribe is idempotent and does not duplicate START, resources or delivery. A distinct callback can acquire another subscription. Each release is bound to its exact registration and cannot remove a later registration. Record acquired release ownership before callbacks. If public subscribe fails before returning and ownership was not transferred, unwind that acquisition; an independently transferred owner retains its cleanup responsibility. Initial/fanout observer errors follow R-operation-failure. During terminal fanout, a queued next-execution request is admitted only after the retiring full array and required close, not attached to a finished registration. Final-owner release is resource lifecycle management, not an upstream protocol unsubscribe message.

Observer-origin output,PAUSE,RESUME,INVALIDATE,PULL,TEARDOWN,subscription and topology requests apply in issue order after the current complete propagation/fanout boundary. PAUSE is queued too; it cannot overtake earlier work. Validate submission without applying its future effects, then recheck origin/target conditions at actual application. A request executes once or is lawfully canceled; callback failure does not strand unrelated queued work. Internal wiring/acquisition and actual fn reentry are distinct surfaces. No graph-global output-payload FIFO or mid-array subscription mutation is implied. Requests from batch early-DIRTY observers wait until the outer batch commit/rollback outcome and its resulting propagation finish; early notification fanout alone is not the application boundary. These observer requests retain independent fate after either outcome.

A ctx belongs to one lifecycle identity. Actual close first enters closing and revokes ordinary ctx/queued-work authority, then synchronously notifies its lifecycle cancellation signal, releases dependencies, runs managed cleanup and required synchronous unwind, finalizes private retention and detaches the old life. Reactivation waits for completion and creates new identity/signal. Old down output is dropped; new state/up/hook/dynamic-read operations through invalid ctx reject, except the narrow managed cleanup read view. Signal access remains bound to the old life, including first access after close returning an aborted old signal. Allocate its native controller lazily; same-life calls share one signal. PAUSE,INVALIDATE and same-life rerun do not abort it. Native listener exceptions follow host semantics; helper owns per-task switching and external cancellation completion.

User fn failures use their designated computation ERROR boundary. Observer, acquisition, cleanup, invalid-operation and checkpoint failures instead follow their owning operation's caller/reporting route; do not turn them into the sender's protocol ERROR automatically. Finish unaffected valid fanout/bookkeeping, attempt independent releases once, preserve primary/cleanup causes and report after internal finalization. No rollback of delivered messages/effects, automatic retry or persistent failure blockade follows. Host-origin operations without a synchronous caller use the configured host reporter. Optional external diagnostics own history; absent a receiver, the node stores no default failure history.

Output acceptance, publication and input consumption are separate facts. Validate before irreversible acceptance; provisional batch intents have not yet applied hooks. Register accepted publication/tail presence before local invalidation hooks. Hold accepted publication in one node-local FIFO/cursor with one runner, and retire entries after valid complete fanout or lawful drop. Update published cache, replay and revision before external callbacks; internal DIRTY prepass still precedes settlement. Fn/buffer return is not publication. Track one actual notification interval, not debt per prefix or async task. Batch rollback may balance only the still-open interval that its own entry actually opened, leaving unrelated pre-existing notification intact. Cache freshness may remain stale after an old result settles notification if newer known input remains unresolved. Output-execution identity distinguishes admitted requests across terminal seal/reset; it is distinct from notification-interval identity and native resource-life identity. Stable manual-input intent preserves its scope across ordinary nonterminal last-off. Reuse logical output identity rather than adding a public epoch counter or historical registry.

Each node maintains monotonic revision and valueRevision evidence independently of optional hashing. revision advances for actual committed output/retained-snapshot transitions: DATA,RESOLVED,effective INVALIDATE,terminal and genuine silent retained-snapshot adoption/reset. valueRevision marks the latest such DATA/value-write/removal; no-event initial/replay/restore installation or resource attachment advances either. Equal DATA remains an occurrence and advances positions. Positions do not reset merely on disconnect; lifecycle/connection scope must be checked before comparisons. Do not maintain an automatic extra DATA-only counter or infer evaluated input from a received revision. Optional canonical hash describes current retained value/absence and stays consistent with silent changes; it is not event identity, freshness proof or a full event log. Save/restore represented evidence unchanged; reject numerical exhaustion rather than silently wrap.

A consumer owns its received value/absence, ended status and received-revision evidence per stable connection, separately from unconsumed projections. Upstream cleanup/restart does not rewrite an already-ended receipt or make it follow the new execution. For supported restore save the compact actual received record, including live quiet-PULL input, rather than reseeding from upstream current cache. Establish recovery comparisons at restore commit, not delayed first subscription; consume/advance the comparison boundary only at the accepted initialization/live-input handoff, not because resources reattach. Reorder retains evidence; remove/re-add and consumer actual close retire the old scope. Unsupported unrepresented pending catch-up rejects capture.

Resource reconstruction after restore uses the existing factory/registered reattach seam, with a new valid lifecycle ctx and normal acquisition/cleanup ownership. It rebuilds resources without a gratuitous normal fn evaluation or replay of captured DATA. Before using a preserved-result exemption, validate restored input/connection evidence and apply the selected latest snapshot refresh when it changed before first attachment; do not manufacture historical live occurrences. A pending reattach belongs to its computation registration: successful fn replacement cancels it, rejected preflight does not. Missing or unsupported reconstruction recipes fail honestly; arbitrary external I/O is not resumed by restoring a buffer.

A message is an array whose first element is its type. The type set is closed: START, PENDING, DATA, RESOLVED, INVALIDATE, COMPLETE and ERROR; any other type is rejected. [DATA, v] carries exactly one non-SENTINEL payload, and [ERROR, e] one non-SENTINEL, non-boolean diagnostic. Messages travel only downstream, from a node to its subscribers and dependents; nothing travels up the graph. Control such as pausing, demand or restart is not a message type: a controller writes a plain state node that its target declares as a dependency, so control is ordinary DATA on a declared edge. The message classes, in order, are START; PENDING; value (DATA, RESOLVED); INVALIDATE; terminal (COMPLETE, ERROR). The kernel never reorders an array by class.
rationale: Kernel concept K1 (D797). Control as data on a declared edge (P11) leaves no upward channel and no control message; TEARDOWN is retired because a lifetime ends at the last unsubscribe. PENDING is the former DIRTY.

statement: A wave starts from one host input to a state node (set, invalidate, complete, error), a batch commit, or a node's ctx.down called after its function returned, and runs to completion before the next request starts. Each ctx.down call is one array. A node's arrays reach each subscriber after its function returned, in order, all of them to one subscriber before the next. PENDING is sent only by the kernel, as the first message of each array that carries DATA or RESOLVED; node output containing PENDING is rejected. Each pending mark is settled exactly once within its wave, by DATA, RESOLVED, INVALIDATE or a terminal; a node that was marked pending and sent nothing gets exactly one RESOLVED from the kernel, the only output the kernel adds. A node's function runs at most once per wave, after every dependency that was marked pending has settled, so a fan-in sees one consistent set of inputs. The kernel delivers every DATA unchanged and in order and never merges, drops, substitutes or reorders it. An array keeps its written order: a terminal is last, DATA and RESOLVED do not share an array, and an array is split at its last INVALIDATE, so what came before it is dropped and the INVALIDATE goes out as its own array. A quiet node consumes its input waves without being marked pending or sending anything, forwards INVALIDATE at once, and publishes its later output as a new wave.
rationale: Kernel concept K2 (D797), from P2-P4, P7 and P9. Kernel-only PENDING (O11) means no pending mark outlives its wave, so no deferred settlement duty exists; written order (O13) keeps the author's last value.

statement: subscribe(sink, node) delivers one first array: START followed by the node's snapshot, which is the DATA values of the last array the node sent that carried any DATA, then its terminal if it has ended. A new dependent receives the snapshot as one input array on its first run. Subscribing activates an inactive node (R-lifetime). A computed node's retained values are cleared by an effective INVALIDATE and by deactivation; a state node keeps its values until INVALIDATE. A node may be given at construction an optional seed of retained values, a terminal and private state, which it holds as if it had produced them; its first activation still runs its function.
rationale: Kernel concept K3 (D797). The array is the unit, so a late subscriber sees what the node last sent; history across arrays is a module node, not a kernel option. The seed serves restore.

statement: A node's function has the shape (ctx) => void. For each dependency i, ctx.deps[i] gives the dependency's id; the arrays it delivered to this invocation, each as its DATA payloads in order (a RESOLVED array is empty), keeping array boundaries; its terminal in this invocation, if any; and the latest value received from it, if any. ctx also gives private state for the current lifetime (state.get, state.set), down for output, an abort signal, and onDeactivation and onInvalidate cleanup registration. ctx.down is the function's only output. A running function is never reentered: a write from a function to one of its own upstream nodes throws. Any other request the function makes waits until the current wave ends (R-request-order).
rationale: Kernel concept K4 (D797), from P7 and P10. Gates, dynamic reads and equality dedup are sugar inside the function, not kernel behavior.

statement: COMPLETE and ERROR end a node's output for good: nothing follows them and the node never runs again. Each kind has an auto or manual policy per node; both default to auto. Auto ERROR: a dependency's ERROR ends the node with that ERROR without running its function. Auto COMPLETE: once every dependency has ended, the node completes after the run that sees the last terminal; a node with no dependencies never completes automatically. Manual: the terminal is given to the function as input, and the node ends only when its function sends a terminal. The policies apply equally to terminals found in snapshots at a lifetime's first run. An ended node can still be subscribed, depended on, and added as a dependency by rewire or replace; its snapshot carries its last values and its terminal. A host input to an ended node is refused, and so is a rewire of it. There is no resubscription: a part that must start again is an inner node that an owner replaces.
rationale: Kernel concept K5 (D797), from P5. The 2x2 policy replaces three booleans (O6); accepting an ended node keeps results independent of subscription timing; restart is a module (O7).

statement: INVALIDATE is effective only at a node that retains a value. An effective INVALIDATE removes the node's retained values and its dependents' records of them, runs the node's onInvalidate hooks with the value already absent, runs no function, and is forwarded to the node's dependents; at a node that retains no value it is dropped, so a cone, including a diamond, is invalidated once. It carries no PENDING and settles a pending mark. It comes from the host invalidating a state node, or from a node's own output; nothing sends it upstream.
rationale: Kernel concept K6 (D797). Upward INVALIDATE is retired with the upward channel; pause's interaction with INVALIDATE belongs to the pause module.

statement: A node is active while it has a subscriber or an active dependent. Activating a computed node acquires its dependencies, activating them, then runs its function once on their snapshots; a state node has no function. Deactivation, when the last subscriber and active dependent leave, releases the node's dependencies, runs its onDeactivation cleanups, aborts its signal, and drops its private state and, for a computed node, its retained values. Every ctx and cleanup belongs to exactly one lifetime. Output or a request made through a ctx whose lifetime has closed is dropped; a cleanup registered after close runs once at once.
rationale: Kernel concept K7 (D797), from P6. A request dies with the innermost scope it was made in, which replaces per-rule wording about old executions.

statement: Requests made while a wave is being delivered (host inputs, subscribe, unsubscribe, replace, rewire, batch), whether from a function, a sink callback or a cleanup, wait until the wave ends and then run in the order they were made. batch(body) runs body, recording its host inputs and topology requests without delivering anything; when body returns, its host inputs commit as one wave, and its topology requests then run in order. A body that throws commits nothing and drops its requests. An async function body is refused before it runs; a body that returns a promise commits its synchronous part, and the host reporter is told that later writes are separate waves. A batch inside a batch body joins the outer one. replace(id, deps, fn) closes the node's current instance and starts a new one under the same id and subscribers, as on a first activation. rewire(id, deps, fn) keeps the instance with its values, private state, lifetime and subscribers: kept dependencies keep their records, removed ones are released silently, and added ones are acquired and their snapshots given to the function as one input wave. Topology requests run only between waves.
rationale: Kernel concept K8 (D797), from P7. Batch delivers nothing before commit (O3), so it has nothing to roll back; rewire between waves (O4) leaves no record in flight when a node changes shape.

statement: A node has a stable id, a kind (state or node), its declared ordered dependencies and, for a computed node, its function. Its status is derived from what it holds, not stored: cache is empty (no retained value), stale (a pending mark it received or sent in the current wave is unsettled) or ready; output is open, completed or errored; lifecycle is inactive, active or closing (its cleanups are running). The graph describes its topology as data: every node in creation order with its id, kind, dependencies and whether it is quiet.
rationale: Kernel concept K10 (D797), from P1. With restart as a module there is no execution layer: node contains lifetime.

statement: A throw from a node's function becomes that node's ERROR. An invalid output array (PENDING in node output, DATA with RESOLVED, a terminal not last, an unknown type) throws from ctx.down; uncaught, that throw is the node's ERROR. Any other failure goes to its caller or, when there is none, to the host reporter, and never into an unrelated node's messages. The host reporter is a callback; the kernel keeps no failure history.
rationale: Kernel concept K11 (D797), from P10.

statement: No imperative side-channel triggers (event emitters, callbacks, setTimeout plus set) drive graph behavior. Coordination flows through messages along declared dependencies; a controller acts on its target only by writing a state node that the target declares as a dependency, so every control relation is a drawable edge. Remove imperative paths when no caller depends on them.
rationale: D797: there is no ctx.up; control is data on a declared edge (P11).

statement: A node is the thinnest primitive: its function, its declared dependencies and its wave state (dependency records, pending marks, retained values, terminal, subscribers, private state), with no inspection data. A bare node works at the kernel level but has no naming, find or describe; those are graph-layer.
rationale: D797: pause lock sets belong to the pause module, not to every node.

statement: Pause is a node placed in the graph, not a node option. A pausable P sits after one input and depends on a lock state: a plain state node whose value is the set of held locks. A controller pauses by adding a lock and resumes by removing it, so each pause or resume is a state write ordered by R-request-order. While any lock is held, P sends no values and holds every array that arrives, in order and keeping its boundaries; when the last lock is released, P sends all held arrays in one wave, each as it arrived. An INVALIDATE reaching P passes at once and discards what P held before it; a terminal passes at once and discards what was held. While no lock is held, P forwards every occurrence unchanged. Placed before a node, P keeps values from the node while paused, and the node runs on resume on every array held since the last INVALIDATE; placed after a node, the node keeps computing and only its output is held. Several pausables may share one lock state, so one resume releases them in one wave. The locks live in the lock state, so they survive the pausable's deactivation and terminal. A source that must stop working declares the lock state as a dependency and starts or stops its own work in its function. Each pause or resume is a wave through P, so downstream receives a PENDING settled by RESOLVED.
rationale: Module rule (D797): it cites only kernel rules and activates separately, after the kernel set. The two TS modes, default pause and resumeAll, become placement before or after the paused node; INVALIDATE is never held, so downstream never receives a value older than an INVALIDATE it already has.

statement: Demand is a holder node placed after one input, with a demand state that its controller writes: each pull writes a fresh demand record carrying optional params. The holder is quiet (R-wave): between pulls it holds the arrays that arrived since the last INVALIDATE and sends nothing, not even PENDING. Each pull runs the holder's service function once, with the held arrays as its input and the pull's params, even when nothing arrived; what it sends goes out as a later wave, and it may send nothing. A service hands over what was held, so the next service sees only what came after. Several pulls in one wave, such as in one batch, are served once with the latest params. A pull made in a batch body is served after the commit, and a throwing body serves nothing. A pull at an inactive holder neither activates it nor is kept: on activation the holder serves only later pulls. An INVALIDATE discards what was held and reaches subscribers at once; the input's terminal ends the holder and discards what was held; deactivation discards it too. A later subscriber receives the last served value in its START, as for any retained value.
rationale: Module rule (D797): it cites only kernel rules and activates separately, after the kernel set. A pull travels on a declared control pair, not by routing upstream (P11), so the builder holds the holder's handle (O14) and no routed-diamond rule is needed.

statement: History is a node over one source whose value is the list of the last n DATA occurrences the source has sent since the history node was activated, oldest first and including equal values; n is a positive integer. On activation the list starts with the source's snapshot. Each source array that carries DATA makes the node send the new list; an array without DATA sends nothing. The list is the node's private state: an INVALIDATE from the source clears the node's value and the list, deactivation drops it, and a checkpoint saves it. The source's terminal ends the history node. Ordinary nodes have no history option; their snapshot is their last array (R-subscription).
rationale: Module rule (D797): it cites only kernel rules and activates separately, after the kernel set. One value that sinks and dependents see alike replaces a per-node replay buffer used only by the occurrence solutions.

statement: A checkpoint is taken only at a wave boundary, when no wave is running and no batch body is open; otherwise capture is refused. It saves the topology in creation order and, for each node, a recipe: a registered factory reference and a JSON configuration, never a function body. A node built without a recipe, or whose dependencies changed after it was built from one, is local-only, and restoring it fails, as does a missing recipe. For each node a checkpoint saves the values of its last array and its terminal; for a computed node with a lifetime, also its private state and what it received from each dependency; a computed node without a lifetime is saved as holding nothing. Values and private state must be JSON. Restore builds a new graph in checkpoint order with no subscribers and runs no function: a state gets its saved values as one array and then its terminal; a computed node gets its saved values, terminal and private state as a construction seed (R-subscription), and an ended node stays ended with its dependencies. At a restored node's first activation, if every dependency still holds what the node had received, its function does not run; otherwise it runs once with only the changed dependencies as input, and a run that sends nothing keeps the saved value. A restored graph captured again before anything subscribes keeps the saved state. Work in flight at capture is lost: it is neither resumed nor re-issued.
rationale: Module rule (D797): it cites only kernel rules and activates separately, after the kernel set. Capture at a wave boundary (O5) needs no pending-queue or receipt capture in the kernel. The refresh on a changed input follows the user's choice over TS, which keeps the restored value until the next change. Revision and hash encoding, namespaces and resource reattach are not yet specified (graphrefly:B140 Checkpoint/encoding).

statement: Restart is an owner node that faces downstream for good, with the part that may end and start again as an inner node at a fixed path under it. The inner depends on long-lived nodes outside the owner through ordinary dependencies, so nothing upstream is resubscribed. The owner forwards the inner's values. Its terminals are manual (R-terminals), so the inner's COMPLETE or ERROR is input to the owner's policy, which either starts a new attempt or ends the owner with that terminal for good; while a restart is possible no terminal reaches downstream. A new attempt replaces the inner (replace, R-request-order): same id and subscribers, a fresh instance, so the topology description is unchanged and the inner's sinks receive START at each attempt. The policy has a number of rounds, how many times the inner may complete, and a retry policy that decides whether and after what delay an ERROR is retried, counted afresh in each round. A restart request from outside is a write to the owner's declared restart state and starts an attempt that counts toward neither. A delayed retry is dropped if the owner's lifetime closed meanwhile. When the owner deactivates without having ended, an ended inner is renewed. No restart is attempted once a dependency of the inner has ended.
rationale: Module rule (D797): it cites only kernel rules and activates separately, after the kernel set. Protocol COMPLETE and ERROR stay final (P5); recoverable endings and attempts belong to the owner (O7), so observation goes on across attempts at a stable path.

statement: Revision evidence is an observer over the nodes it is given, not node state. For each node it keeps revision, which advances once per committed DATA, RESOLVED, INVALIDATE, COMPLETE or ERROR the node sends, and valueRevision, the revision of the latest DATA or INVALIDATE. The START snapshot is installation, not an event, so subscribing, restore and late subscribers advance neither; PENDING is not output; an equal DATA counts; an INVALIDATE that removes nothing is never sent, so it does not count. The observer is a real subscriber: it activates a node and keeps it active, so its positions do not reset on disconnect while it runs. Its positions can be saved as JSON and a new observer started from them, so saving them beside a checkpoint keeps them unchanged across restore. An optional hash describes the node's current retained values, or their absence, and is computed when read, so it always agrees with the snapshot; it is not event identity or proof of freshness. A position never wraps: an array that would take revision past the largest safe integer is refused whole, leaving the positions unchanged, and the failure goes to the host reporter.
rationale: Module rule (D797): it cites only kernel rules and activates separately, after the kernel set. Revision evidence as an observer (O9): a whole-graph restore at a wave boundary needs no comparison, and a live external source is compared by its own DATA-level version. There is no automatic DATA-only counter. The hash's canonical encoding is open (graphrefly:B140 Checkpoint/encoding).
